data.title: Brodské – Veleš, a hillfort and the puzzles of its dating
data.excerpt: The study of early occupation sometimes comes down to dealing with awkward situations: the same finds dated differently by different specialists, or located to the wrong village altogether. Brodské is such a case – a hillfort in the locality of Veleš, named after the Slavic god Veles, which probably guarded the southern approach route to Břeclav-Pohansko.
data.metaTitle: Brodské – Veleš, a hillfort and its dating puzzles
data.metaDescription: The site of Brodské-Veleš shows how differing dating and the unclear location of finds complicate the study of early occupation in Záhorie.

children.text: The study of historical occupation requires, among other things, a good command of problematic situations. Complications can be brought into the study of occupation, for example, by the differing chronological attribution of the same archaeological finds by different specialists, or by their unclear location. Brodské is such an example.

The literature often (unfortunately even today) cites finds from a cremation cemetery that were supposed to have come from the cadastral area of the village of Brodské (the locality of Trnava). These are four cremation urns and two smaller vessels from the 7th–8th centuries, found in 1922 and 1937. Besides Brodské, however, their discovery is also located to Lanžhot in Moravia. The most recent conclusions say that it is neither Brodské nor Lanžhot, but that these cemetery finds in fact come from the cadastral area of the town of Břeclav.

North-west of the built-up area of Brodské lies the locality of Veleš. The name itself points to an old Slavic origin, derived from the name of Veles, protector of herds, god of abundance and fertility and ruler of the afterlife. In 1976 building work here disturbed dwellings with stone foundations and Slavic sherds were found. This occupation was interpreted as a hillfort and dated to the 9th–10th centuries. According to the account of Konštantín Jakubec, during amateur digging at Veleš a few years before the find mentioned above (around 1970) he came upon a hillfort encircled by a ditch and ramparts, a great many sherds and charcoal, and he located the entrance gateway of the hillfort. About 300 m from the hillfort stands a rotunda, beside which he dug up 10 graves. Proceeding from its position by the river Morava not far from the hillfort of Břeclav-Pohansko, and from the name of the village derived from the word brod (ford), a guard function for the hillfort could be considered. It may have guarded the southern approach route to Pohansko. Unfortunately this site has not been investigated professionally and systematically, and it is therefore difficult to put forward any further hypotheses about it.

Two important routes ran through Záhorie, and from the second third of the 9th century these acquired a considerably wider significance. They became the links between the central settlements of Great Moravia. The first entered Záhorie through the Buková Pass and in two branches, by way of Šaštín and Senica, headed for Mikulčice. The second route, along the Morava, ran from Bratislava and Devín by way of Stupava to Kúty and at Brodské it crossed the river Morava and continued on to Pohansko. These routes were linked transversely by a road from Brodské and Kúty running by way of Stráže to Senica, where it joined the Jablonica–Holíč road.

children.text:
This is also why the presence of warriors in Skalica, in Brodské and in Kopčany – on the left bank of the river Morava – in the 9th century can be explained by their protective function on these routes in front of the Great Moravian centres (Břeclav-Pohansko, Mikulčice-Valy, Uherské Hradiště-Staré Město). The hillfort at Veleš is one of the two archaeologically attested Great Moravian hillforts in Záhorie (together with the hillfort of Podbranč-Starý hrad). The hypothetical possibility that two further hillforts existed in the 9th century rests on linguistic evidence (Hradište pod Vrátnom, Brezová pod Bradlom-Hrádok). The case of Zámčisko near Unín remains unresolved. 
 “The parish and the church are mentioned as early as 1163,” Konštantín Palkovič writes of Brodské. The information comes from Ľudovít Némethy, who refers to older schematisms. Unfortunately the original written document is not known. The name Veleš suggests a pagan cult. The Christian church was perhaps meant to suppress the pagan religious relics to which the inhabitants of Záhorie may to some extent have returned after the demise of Great Moravia. The occupation of this region, however, is known to us only from neighbouring Kúty, and that is dated to the 10th–11th centuries. The history of Brodské from the 10th to the 13th century therefore remains without historical or archaeological evidence. In 1989 sherd material was recovered from Veleš by field survey which might attest to a deserted settlement. The sherds were found over a relatively large area (3 ha) and were from the 13th–14th centuries. In 1317 Abrahám Rúfus acquired Šaštín (Saswar) together with Brodské (Barachka, Baracka). King Charles granted them to him as compensation for the damage he had suffered at the hands of Matúš Čák. The Šaštín comitatus is mentioned in 1323. That is to say, the castle had its district established. Later we know that the villages on both sides of the Myjava belonged here – Brodské, Borský Mikuláš, Bílkové Humence, Borský Peter, Šajdíkové Humence, Čáry, Dojč, Koválov, Kuklov, Kúty, Smolinské, Stráže, Šaštín and Štefanov. The seat of the Šaštín estate later passed to Holíč.

this interesting legend is recorded, which is attached to the hillfort of Veleš and reaches back as far as the time of Great Moravia:

When Saints Cyril and Methodius were coming to Great Moravia, they were caught in their sleep at night by a flood caused by the waters of the river Morava. Local fishermen led them across the ford to dry land. The name of the village of Brodské comes from the ford. In the historically preserved coat of arms of the village, which builds on an older village seal, it is precisely these two saints who are depicted.
